artworks.title: The Farewell of Telemachus and Eucharis
artworks.description: David's late Neoclassical oil (J. Paul Getty Museum) shows Telemachus parting from the nymph Eucharis on Calypso's island — an episode drawn from Fénelon's Télémaque rather than Homer, yet inseparable from the modern image of Odysseus's son. Painted in Brussels in 1818, the canvas pairs the youth's averted resolve with Eucharis's clinging embrace under cool, sculptural light. It is among the most famous post-Homeric portraits of Telemachus as a sentimental hero of education and duty.

artworks.title: The Sorrow of Telemachus
artworks.description: Angelica Kauffman's Metropolitan Museum canvas (1783) finds Telemachus grieving on Calypso's shore, mentored by Athena in the guise of Mentor — again the Fénelon Telemachy that eighteenth-century Europe read as a mirror for princes. Soft colour and measured gesture turn the Homeric son's search for Odysseus into a lesson in virtuous melancholy. Paired with her companion piece of the nymphs of Calypso, the painting fixed Telemachus as a subject of Grand Tour sensibility.

artworks.title: Telemachus and the Nymphs of Calypso
artworks.description: In this Metropolitan Museum pendant of 1782, Kauffman stages Telemachus among Calypso's nymphs — the island episode from Fénelon's Les Aventures de Télémaque in which the son nearly forgets Ithaca. Pastoral landscape and graceful grouping translate Homeric wandering into Rococo-Neoclassical charm. Together with The Sorrow of Telemachus, the pair became a staple of Anglophone collecting and of Telemachus's afterlife beyond the Odyssey's first four books.

films.title: The Odyssey
films.description: The miniseries follows Telemachus from the suitors' hall to Menelaus' court and back — the son's search for news of his father as the Odyssey's second spine.

films.title: Ulysses
films.description: Camerini's peplum keeps Telemachus in the Ithacan climax — the boy who helps string the bow and clear the hall beside the beggar who is his father.

popCulture.title: Les Aventures de Télémaque
popCulture.creator: François Fénelon
popCulture.description: Fénelon's pedagogical romance sends Telemachus wandering with Mentor — the Homeric son rewritten as a mirror for princes, and one of the most-read books of the eighteenth century.

popCulture.title: Telemachy
popCulture.description: Scholars still call Odyssey books 1–4 the Telemachy — the son's story named as its own epic unit inside the father's.
